Copper-catalyzed perfluoroalkylation of propargyl
gem-dichlorides†
Bosheng Liu, a Jinxu Dong, a Qi Zhu, a Jundong Zhang, a Jian Huang, a Shiwen Liu
 b
and Xiaojun Zeng
 *a
Herein, we present a highly eﬃcient copper-catalyzed protocol for
transforming propargyl gem-dichlorides into the corresponding
chloro-substituted fluoroalkylated allenes. This protocol demon-
strates a broad substrate scope and excellent tolerance towards
various functional groups. Moreover, the strategy of utilizing the
chloro-substituted pentafluoroethylation allenes for multiple trans-
formations has shown significant value in synthetic chemistry.
Given the unique properties and reactivity of the cumulated diene
system, allenes hold significant importance in organic synthesis,
serving as versatile intermediates in functional group transfor-
mations.
1 Moreover, allenes are prevalent in natural products, bioac-
tive small molecules, and functional materials.2 It is widely recognized
that incorporating a fluoroalkyl group into pharmaceutical candidates
often enhances various medicinal properties, such as significantly
influencing binding aﬃnity, improving bioavailability, enhancing
membrane permeability, and providing protection againstin vivo
metabolism.3 Therefore, the development of eﬃcient methods for
synthesizing diverse fluoroalkylated allenes4 is evidently of great value.
These methods facilitate scaﬀold modification to meet the evolving
demands of drug discovery and material development.
Modern approaches for the synthesis of fluoroalkylated
allenes typically involve copper-mediated or -catalyzed cross-
coupling of propargylic electrophiles with appropriate fluor-
oalkyl reagents. For instance, Qing,
5 Szabo,6 Xiao,7 and
Nishibayashi8 independently report copper-mediated or
-catalyzed trifluoromethylation of various propargylic electro-
philes, including propargylic halides, acetates, and methane-
sulfonates, using appropriate nucleophilic CF
3 reagents to
aﬀord trisubstituted trifluoromethylallenes. Along this line,
Shen
9 developed a copper catalyzed difluoromethylation of
propargyl bromides using their invented CF 2H reagents. How-
ever, existing methods often require stoichiometric amounts of
copper. Additionally, fluoroalkylated allenes bearing only alkyl
or aryl groups lack versatility for further transformations,
thereby limiting the diversity of the synthesized fluoroalkylated
allene scaﬀolds. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge,
approaches to perfluoroalkylated ( e.g.,C
nFn+1, n Z 2) allenes
are underexplored, despite the perfluoroalkyl moiety also pos-
sessing some unique properties. 10 Given the widespread appli-
cation of cross electrophile-coupling strategies, chloro-
substituted allenes serve as versatile coupling partners, 11 pro-
viding facile access to diverse allene scaﬀolds. Therefore, eﬀorts
to synthesize more active chlorinated fluoroalkylated allene
products are desirable. Propargyl gem-dichlorides (Scheme 1b)
have garnered significant attention from chemists due to their

catalyzed tri/difluoromethylation of propargyl (pseudo)halides. (b) Copper-
catalyzed functionalization of propargylgem-dichlorides. (c) This work.

versatile activity. The resulting product, containing a chlorine atom,
holds particular interest as it all ows for further transformations
compared to allenes bearing only alkyl or aryl groups. For example,
the Alexakis group12 reported copper-catalyzed 1,3-substitution of
propargyl gem-dichloride substrates with readily available nucleo-
philic Grignard reagents, yielding chlorinated allenes. Following
this research direction, the Toh/Xu group
13 employed propargyl
gem-dichlorides to synthesize chloro-substituted allenylsilanes in
the presence of a copper catalyst using a compatible PhMe2Si-Bpin
reagent. More recently, the Xu group14 demonstrated that catalytic
copper enables the borylation of propargylgem-dichlorides for the
synthesis of chlorosubstituted allenyl-Bdan products. Despite the
growing interest in preparing va rious functional chlorinated
allenes, methods to achieve chlor o-substituted fluoroalkylated
allenes remain relatively underexplored. Inspired by the pioneering
work of the Knochel group
15 (Scheme 1c) on propargyl gem-
dichlorides for copper-mediated cross-coupling reactions with alkyl
zinc reagents, we were motivated to investigate the possibility of a
copper-catalyzed perfluoroalkylation of propargylgem-dichlorides
using suitable (DMPU)
2Zn(Rf)2 reagents.
To test the validity of this hypothesis, propargyl gem-
dichloride ( 1), prepared from the corresponding propargylic
aldehyde, was selected as the model substrate for investigating
the reaction conditions (Table 1). Following a thorough opti-
mization campaign, it was determined that in the presence of
catalytic amounts of CuCl (10 mol%), phenanthroline ligand L
3
(10 mol%), and 0.8 equiv. of znic-C 2F5 reagent 2, facilitated the
eﬀective transformation of compound 1 into the chloro-
substituted pentafluoroethylated allenes 3. This transformation
was achieved with an impressive yield of 92% at room tempera-
ture in 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE) (entry 1). The use of the other
copper salts such as Cu(
I)o rC u ( II), resulted in a significantly
decreased yield (entries 2 and 3), while replacing the copper catalyst
with a nickel catalyst did not yield desirable products (entry 4).
Further exploration into the comme rcially available nucleophilic
C2F5 reagents revealed that thein situ generation of CuC2F5 species
i nt h ep r e s e n c eo fT M S C2F5 was slower compared to the use of
(DMPU)2Zn(C2F5)2, which exhibited superior reactivity (entry 5).
The reaction had deleterious eﬀects on the coupling reactions
when equal amounts of the C
2F5 source were used (entry 6). Among
the commercially available ligands, 2,9-dimethyl-1,10-phenanthro-
line ligand proved to be the most eﬀective, while other ligands,
including bipyridine or tridentate ligands (2,2 0:60,200-terpyridine)
were less eﬀective (entries 7 and 8). Solvents play an important role
in this pentafluoroethylation reaction; replacing DCE with other
solvents led to diminished yields (entries 9–11). Control reactions
supported our proposed mechanism, with no conversion occurring
in the absence of Cu or ligand (entries 12 and 13). Interestingly,
even when the reaction was conducted in an open-air environment,
only a minor decrease in the yield was observed (entry 13).
With these optimized conditions established, a broad range
of propargyl gem-dichlorides were used as an electrophile to
install a pentafluoroethyl group on the chloroallenic moiety
(Table 2). Substrates featuring diverse aryl groups were eﬃ-
ciently converted into the respective chloro-substituted penta-
fluoroethylated allenes, yielding high amounts of product
quantities with notable selectivity ( 3–16). Generally, as the
electron density on the aromatic ring increased, the efficiency
of this transformation tended to rise. For example, the ortho-
substituted electron-rich groups, such as methyl 4 and alkoxy
(5, 6), exhibited higher yields compared to electron-deficit
groups like cyano 7 and nitro 8. However, aryl substitution
with an electron-donating group at the para position furnished
the corresponding products in lower yields ( 11, 12). A diverse
range of synthetic handles showed good tolerance to the
reaction, including ketone 13, and ester 14. Substrates bearing
halogens such as Cl and Br ( 9, 10, 15) were well accommodated,
enabling further modification of pentafluoroethylation pro-
ducts. Moreover, the current copper-catalyzed process shows
the much larger substrate scope than the previous copper
catalyzed process,
14b where the aryl substituted propargyl
gem-dichlorides led to no reported results.
Next, we explored the substrate scope of this reaction by using a
series of alkyl substituted propargylgem-dichlorides. It was observed
that substrates containing electron-rich alkylbenzene rings had a
minimal eﬀect on the reaction (17, 18). As expected, substrates with
diﬀerent primary alkyl groups, such asn-decanyl21,c h l o r i d e22and
alkene 25, exerted a deleterious eﬀect on the reaction. However,
substrates with functional groups such as phenol19,s i l y le t h e r24,
acetal26,a n dc a r b a z o l e27 groups were all compatible to aﬀord the
corresponding products. Remarkably, pentafluoroethylation of a
radical clock cyclopropane substituentgem-dichloride aﬀorded the
desirable product23 rather than the ring opening product, indicat-
ing that this process did not involve a radical intermediate.
Given the value of CF
2H as a bioisostere of the thiol and
amino groups, 16 we proceeded to investigate the extension
of this reaction to the difluoromethylation of the propargyl

strates bearing aromatic and aliphatic groups smoothy deliv-
ered adducts 28–30 with good efficiency (55–81% yield).
Furthermore, we investigated whether this method could be
expanded to install longer-chain perfluoroalkyl groups. To
achieve this, (DMPU)
2Zn(CnF2n+1)2
18 were employed as compa-
tible Rf reagents, yielding the corresponding chloro-substituted
fluoroalkylated allenes with useful efficiencies. Trifluoromethy-
lation ( 31–33), heptafluoropropylation ( 34–36), nonafluorobu-
tylation ( 37–39) and perfluorohexylation ( 40–42) effectively
demonstrated the versatility of this protocol, representing a
novel and straightforward approach for introducing diverse
perfluoroalkyl groups onto chloro-substituted allenes.
To further showcase the potential utility of the synthesized
chloro-substituted fluoroalkylated allenes, their subsequent
conversion into diverse fluoroalkylated compounds can be
achieved through simple one-step operation (Scheme 2). For
example, the chloro-substituted allene 21 c o u l db eu t i l i z e dt o
produce pentafluoroethylated compound43 via Suzuki coupling
reaction with potassium vinyltri fluoroborate. Similarly, the

chlorinated allenes17 could be subjected to a Sonogashira coupling
reaction, resulting in the pro duction of 1,3-diyne products 44.
Additionally, chlorinated allenes24 can be transformed into the
corresponding difluoromethylated45 through a copper-catalyzed
coupling reaction. Furthermore, the palladium-catalyzed coupling
reaction of chlorinated allenes27 with phenylboronic acid provided
compound46 in good yield.
Based on the presented results and literature reports, 19 we
proposed a possible mechanism (please see ESI, † Scheme S1).
The [Cu1-Rf] intermediate is hypothesized to be generated in situ
through a transmetalation between (DMPU)2Zn(Rf)2 reagent and
CuI(I). Subsequently, in the presence of propargylgem-dichlorides, a
p-complex intermediate B was formed in situ.F o l l o w i n gt h i s ,a
divergent pathway may occur: either a fluoroalkyl copper anion
attack on the acetylene carbon, leading to an S
N2020 substitution to
form copper( III)i n t e r m e d i a t eC, or an anti-selective addition
occurred, resulting in copper( I)i n t e r m e d i a t eD.S u b s e q u e n t l y ,
reductive elimination from C or b-elimination from D yields the
target chloro-substituted fluoroalkylated allenes3, with the copper
catalyst being released for the next catalytic cycle.
In conclusion, we have developed a novel method for the
copper-catalyzed cross-coupling of propargyl gem-dichlorides
with (DMPU)2Zn(Rf)2 to assemble chloro-substituted fluoroalky-
lated allenes. The reaction proceeded under mild conditions
and exhibited good tolerance towards various functional
groups. The introduction of fluoroalkyl onto chlorinated
allenes, allowing transition metal-catalyzed cross-coupling,
serves as an important scaﬀold to be further transformed to
trisubstituted allenes. Due to its simplicity, this methodology
demonstrates broad applicability in the preparation of mole-
cules containing fluoroalkylated groups.
